walkthroughs.body_html: GDP is the total value of all goods and services produced in a country in a year. Three ways to calculate: output, income or expenditure — all give the same answer in theory. UK GDP ~£2.5 trillion (2024).

Nominal uses current prices — can rise just because prices rose. Real strips out inflation, showing genuine output change. If nominal grows 5% but inflation is 3%, real growth is only 2%. Always use real GDP to compare years.
1) Boom — rapid growth, low unemployment, rising inflation. 2) Recession — two quarters of falling GDP. 3) Slump/trough — bottom. 4) Recovery — growth restarts. Cycles last ~5–10 years on average.

Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP
Inflation above 5%
Unemployment above 10%

options: Total country size only
Average living standards
Inflation rate
Number of workers

mcqs.q: How is economic growth shown on a Production Possibility Curve?
options: Growth is shown by the curve becoming straighter.
Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
By an outward shift of the entire curve — reflecting an increase in productive capacity through more or better resources, technology, or skills.
Growth is shown by moving from inside the curve to a point on the curve.
Inflation is when prices are high.
Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
Growth is shown by the curve becoming straighter.
A sustained rise in the general price level over time — reducing the purchasing power of money. Measured by the percentage change in a price index.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between fixed and variable costs?
options: Fixed costs never change at all, ever.
Growth is shown by the curve becoming straighter.
Fixed costs don't change with output (e.g. rent, salaries); variable costs change directly with output (e.g. raw materials, hourly wages).
Fixed costs are paid once and variable costs are paid daily.
